rows.question: What changed in Sonatype's pricing this year?

answer.question: What changed in Sonatype's pricing this year?
answer.standalone_question: What changed in Sonatype's pricing this year?
answer.intro: Three Sonatype pricing-page changes are logged for 2026: April, July and October.

points.lead: Oct 21: Cloud Pro rises to $1,950/year
points.text: Nexus Repository Cloud Pro is now $1,950/year plus consumption, up from $1,620. A Self-Hosted Pro Edition at $7,500/year was added, and Cloud plans split into Pro, Pro+ and Enterprise.

points.lead: Oct 21: Several entries removed from page
points.text: Firewall Enterprise, Lifecycle and SBOM Manager entries no longer appear on Sonatype's pricing page.

points.lead: Jul 29: Repricing of Nexus Repository and Firewall
points.text: Nexus Repository now starts at $1,620/year plus consumption, replacing $135/month. Repository Firewall is $4,800/year, previously $18.67 per user/month.

points.lead: Jul 29: Lifecycle custom, new Guide tier
points.text: Lifecycle moved to custom pricing, previously $57.50 per user/month. A new Guide tier starts at $1,200/year.

points.lead: Apr 14: Renaming and bundling, no prices
points.text: Premium became 'Nexus Repository + Repository Firewall', Free became Community Edition, and the Pro offer was renamed. No dollar amounts appeared in the diff, so this looks like packaging, not price.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: Sonatype's higher entry prices and flat Firewall pricing change how Artifactory, Xray and Curation should be compared in deals. Battlecards should also reflect the packaging shifts around Firewall and Lifecycle.

answer.question: Who launched a package firewall?
answer.intro: GitHub launched a package firewall; Sonatype added firewall-style blocking to Nexus Repository.

points.lead: GitHub launched a package firewall preview
points.text: GitHub launched a package firewall in public preview for all GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers, including data-resident deployments. It sits between endpoints such as Actions runners or coding agents and upstream registries.

points.lead: GitHub's firewall is npm-only and free for now
points.text: It supports only npm packages and is free during preview, moving to metered billing at general availability.

points.lead: Sonatype added Firewall to Nexus Repository
points.text: Sonatype announced new Firewall capabilities in Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise editions that screen requests for packages, containers, LLMs and MCP servers and can block malicious, vulnerable or out-of-policy components.

points.lead: Sonatype Nexus tiers block malicious packages
points.text: Nexus Repository Pro+ and Enterprise add malicious package protection and configurable policies to block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: Both moves target JFrog Curation's block-at-entry gate. Position Curation's broader package-format coverage and mature policy engine against GitHub's npm-only preview, and update battlecards against Nexus's new tiers.

rows.question: What supply-chain security incidents happened recently?

answer.question: What supply-chain security incidents happened recently?
answer.standalone_question: What supply-chain security incidents happened recently?
answer.intro: Two recent incidents appear in the documents: a GitHub Actions campaign and a malicious npm release.

points.lead: **GitHub account hijack hit 30,000 repos**
points.text: Attackers accessed roughly 1,900 GitHub accounts and inserted credential-stealing workflows into more than 30,000 repositories, with the largest push on October 8 and 9.

points.lead: **Stolen secrets: CI/CD, cloud and AI keys**
points.text: The malicious GitHub Actions jobs targeted CI/CD secrets, cloud access keys and AI provider API keys and sent them to an attacker-controlled server. GitGuardian tracked the campaign.

points.lead: **Older malicious workflows were recycled**
points.text: The campaign reused older malicious workflows that GitHub's approval controls had not fully removed.

points.lead: **Malicious tensorlake npm release**
points.text: Release tensorlake@0.5.144 used an install hook to search for developer credentials and accept remote commands, per Sonatype's review (reported 2026-10-08).

points.lead: **TensorLake impact not confirmed**
points.text: Sonatype found a GitHub fallback that could create a public repository and commit collected data. It has not confirmed that stolen data was published or that downstream systems were affected.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: Exposed registry tokens and cloud keys from CI pipelines affect Artifactory and Xray users, so JFrog Advanced Security secrets detection and JFrog Curation can be pitched on pipeline secret hygiene and malicious package blocking.

rows.question: What did GitHub change in secret scanning?

answer.question: What did GitHub change in secret scanning?
answer.standalone_question: What did GitHub change in secret scanning?
answer.intro: GitHub changed secret scanning features on 2026-10-20 and its AI detection pricing on 2026-10-21.

points.lead: Revocation extended to encoded GitHub tokens
points.text: GitHub's 2026-10-20 changelog extends the revocation action to encoded GitHub tokens in secret scanning.

points.lead: Custom-pattern alerts stay open on rescan
points.text: Open custom-pattern alerts now stay open when a rescan still matches an edited pattern. Invalid custom pattern API requests return 422 instead of 500.

points.lead: Dismissal webhooks and audit log changes
points.text: Dismissal-request webhooks gain a repository-scoped request number. The business field in certain audit log events changes from display name to slug on November 12, 2026.

points.lead: AI detection split into two add-ons
points.text: GitHub's pricing page replaced the single 'Copilot secret scanning' add-on with 'AI detection for alerts' and 'AI detection for push protection', both usage-based.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: GitHub is raising the baseline for secrets scanning on alert handling and revocation. JFrog Advanced Security can contrast the separately priced AI add-ons with artifact-level security in a platform integration pitch.

rows.question: How is Sonatype talking about AI agents choosing dependencies?

answer.question: How is Sonatype talking about AI agents choosing dependencies?
answer.standalone_question: How is Sonatype talking about AI agents choosing dependencies?
answer.intro: Sonatype frames agent-chosen dependencies as a governance and evidence problem.

points.lead: Agents choose dependencies; accountability follows
points.text: Sonatype's 2026-10-01 blog says coding agents now choose open source dependencies. Teams must track which agent introduced each one, why, and who owns it.

points.lead: Framed as a governance gap
points.text: A 2026-09-24 post says agents select packages, versions and configurations without developer review. It recommends live dependency intelligence, policy before execution, decision provenance and continuous monitoring.

points.lead: Policy at the point of selection
points.text: A 2026-09-29 post recommends embedding policy controls at the point of dependency selection. It says Sonatype Guide and Firewall enforce component policy in developer and AI-assisted workflows.

points.lead: 'AI noise' argument backed by research
points.text: Sonatype cites about 37,000 upgrade recommendations in its 2026 State of the Software Supply Chain research. LLM-generated ones gave the smallest security gain and worsened security in 345 cases. It urges grounding AI in live data.

points.lead: Repository positioned as AI trust gate
points.text: Sonatype positions Nexus Repository as the first-line trust gate for open source, containers, LLMs and MCP servers. It pitches AI-agent dependency governance and malware research, promoting Guide, Firewall and Lifecycle.

rows.question: What did Sonatype's Q3 malware report find?

answer.question: What did Sonatype's Q3 malware report find?
answer.standalone_question: What did Sonatype's Q3 malware report find?
answer.intro: Sonatype's Q3 2026 Open Source Malware Index, published 2026-10-08, reported the following.

points.lead: **149,329 malicious packages logged in Q3**
points.text: Sonatype Research Labs logged 149,329 malicious open source packages in Q3 2026, bringing the total since 2017 to 1,960,846.

points.lead: **npm dominates at 89.5%**
points.text: npm accounted for 89.5% of the quarter's malicious packages, which the evidence quote puts at 133,579 packages.

points.lead: **Droppers and secrets exfiltration prevalent**
points.text: 74.5% of packages with overt-malware behavior involved droppers, secrets exfiltration, or both.

points.lead: **Report supports Sonatype's threat-intel positioning**
points.text: The FrogRadar battlecard lists the index as a Sonatype strength that supports its threat-intelligence positioning.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: The npm-heavy, dropper and credential-theft findings map to JFrog Curation's block-at-entry gate and JFrog Xray's malicious package detection. JFrog battlecards should account for Sonatype's research-led narrative.

rows.question: Is GitHub moving into license compliance?

answer.question: Is GitHub moving into license compliance?
answer.standalone_question: Is GitHub moving into license compliance?
answer.intro: Yes: GitHub made license compliance generally available on 2026-10-16.

points.lead: License compliance is now generally available
points.text: GitHub made open source license compliance generally available for GitHub Enterprise Cloud, including data-resident GHEC, for repositories with GitHub Code Security enabled.

points.lead: Enterprise-wide policy enforced via rulesets
points.text: The feature adds an enterprise-wide license policy enforced through rulesets, with a new 'Require license compliance results before merging' condition.

points.lead: Checks move earlier, aimed at coding agents
points.text: GitHub also added a new API for checking package compliance aimed at coding agents, moving license checks earlier in developer workflows.

points.lead: Part of a wider supply-chain push
points.text: GitHub is adding supply-chain controls such as a package firewall and license gating. The firewall is in public preview, supports only npm, and is free during preview before metered billing at GA.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: JFrog Xray and JFrog Advanced Security now face a native GitHub alternative for PR-time license gating. Battlecards should address enterprise policy enforcement at the pull request stage.

rows.question: What are Sonatype's weaknesses compared to JFrog?

answer.question: What are Sonatype's weaknesses compared to JFrog?
answer.standalone_question: What are Sonatype's weaknesses compared to JFrog?
answer.intro: Battlecard weaknesses and pricing signals point to cost, packaging and tier-gating issues for Sonatype.

points.lead: Malicious-package blocking is tier-gated
points.text: Malicious-package blocking in Nexus is limited to the new Pro+ and Enterprise editions, so lower tiers do not get it.

points.lead: Entry cost has risen
points.text: Nexus Repository Cloud Pro rose to $1,950/year plus consumption from $1,620, and a self-hosted Pro tier is listed at $7,500/year, raising entry cost.

points.lead: Pricing and packaging keep shifting
points.text: Firewall moved from per-user to flat annual pricing and Lifecycle went to custom pricing. Later, Firewall Enterprise, Lifecycle and SBOM Manager no longer appeared on the pricing page.

points.lead: Repricing changed Firewall and Lifecycle terms
points.text: On 2026-07-29 Sonatype's page showed Firewall starting at $4,800/year, previously $18.67 per user/month, and Lifecycle moved to custom pricing, previously $57.50 per user/month.

points.lead: Tier naming was reshuffled
points.text: In April 2026 Sonatype renamed its Nexus Repository tiers, with 'Premium' becoming 'Nexus Repository + Repository Firewall'. The diff showed no dollar amounts, so these were naming and packaging updates.

meaning_for_jfrog.text: JFrog sales can contrast Sonatype's tier-gated blocking, higher entry prices and shifting packaging with Artifactory plus Curation. Note that Sonatype's Pro+ and Enterprise blocking overlaps Curation's entry-point policy gate.
